Its tone sits between bright and dark, with a distinctive metallic quality and depth of resonance. The instrument works on the membranophone principle: a stretched animal skin is struck, and the air inside the resonating body gives the timbre a warm foundation. Its range is wide, from deep and thick to clear and bright. Compared with drums, which are blunt and heavy, the tar's timbre is finer and more elegant; compared with the brass gong, its sound is more intimate. The timbre penetrates yet accommodates: it can stand alone in a solo and show its character, and it can also blend into a band to create a lively sound.

The tar is an Iranian chordophone of the lute family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.321-6, found in West Asia, Central Asia and the Caucasus. The body is double-bellied or hourglass-shaped, made of mulberry, with a membrane over the soundboard: sheepskin on the Persian tar, cow-heart membrane on the Azerbaijani one. It has a long neck with a flat fretboard and adjustable gut frets; the Persian tar has three double courses, the Caucasian one eleven strings including bass drones. It is held high against the chest and played with a brass pick, up and down strokes with a tremolo, while the left hand stops the strings. It is used in Persian music and the radif and mugham, while Azerbaijani music uses the Azerbaijani tar.
塔爾琴演奏時將琴身高置於胸前，右手持小黃銅撥片於琴身中央撥弦，以連續上撥、下撥與: The tar is held high against the chest. The right hand holds a small brass pick and plucks at the centre of the body with continuous downstrokes, upstrokes and a two-way tremolo; the left hand stops the strings on the fretboard to choose the notes and, where needed, bends the string with the stopping finger to change pitch. The Persian tar usually has three double courses and one outer bass string, each string with its own peg and tuned independently; the Azerbaijani tar has eleven playing strings plus side bass strings and sympathetic strings. A beginner can work through holding the instrument, tuning, right-hand picking and left-hand stopping in that order, watching the position of the adjustable gut frets and the angle of the pick.
塔爾琴為伊朗弦鳴樂器，屬魯特琴家族，早期稱四弦琴，以弦數命名；流行於西亞、中亞與: The tar is an Iranian chordophone of the lute family, called the four-string instrument in early sources after its number of strings; it is played in West Asia, Central Asia and the Caucasus, including Iran, Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan, Georgia, Armenia, Tajikistan and Turkey. After its range was adjusted in the eighteenth century it became an important instrument of Iranian and Caucasian music and is used in the radif and the muqam. Around 1870 Sadigjan developed the Azerbaijani tar, and in 2012 its craft and playing were inscribed on the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage.
塔爾琴為弦鳴樂器，常見於西亞、中亞與高加索的音樂場合，包括伊朗、亞塞拜然、烏茲別: The tar is a chordophone found in musical settings across West Asia, Central Asia and the Caucasus, including Iran, Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan, Georgia, Armenia, Tajikistan and Turkey. It is important in Persian music, while Azerbaijani music uses the Azerbaijani tar; it is also the first choice for the radif and the mugham. Armenians also play mugham repertoire on the tar and the kamancha. In contemporary work, Jeff Wayne's 《Musical Version of The War of the Worlds》 uses a tar in the passage “Horsell Common and the Heat Ray”.

The fretboard carries adjustable gut frets, and the head has wooden tuning pegs. The Persian tar uses steel and copper-wound strings plus a copper-wound bass string; the Azerbaijani tar has a small metal nut and a string holder at the tail. The pick is brass.
